sections.title: Chairman's Chat
sections.content:
Tam (AKA Glorious Leader) reports

Well your new committee got off to a good start at the January meeting at the Red Lion in Burley.  A forced absence for Rob lead to us phoning him then linking up via WhatsApp via a laptop. Excellent reception meant that he could hear and be heard pretty clearly. Several years ago we tried with committee members phoning in and it was pretty much a waste of time, with them struggling to hear and getting about 20% of any conversation. It looks like we now have a workable solution, meaning that those who find it difficult to get to a meeting can still join it and contribute. I think we have more technical skills on the committee than before! Happy days.

Amongst other discussions, the Farmer’s Dinner, AGM and the First Aid course were all thought to have been successful club events, so you can expect more of the same this year. The more the merrier for these events so if you are curious about them, why not come along and see what you’ve been missing!  Unfortunately, due to a combination of factors the repack had to be cancelled - this was not simply because of lack of numbers, though this was obviously a factor. Repacking your reserve is an important safety issue, and for those who still need to do it for the coming season, our neighbours at Pennine SC will accept Dales members at their repack in Chipping on March 1st, cost is £30 - contact Barry Sayer barrysayer72@gmail.com .  We are also now investigating more options for next year’s repack, perhaps developing our own qualified repacker. Please read Rob’s piece below and be ready to contribute to his survey to help take things forward.

On the flying side of things, my hatebook feed is now full of reports from around the world of people getting away for winter flying. Some in serious competitions (well done Rich Meek with his task win at the Colombian Open!), others on guided tours in Africa or South America, and others simply enjoying themselves in Australia. What a sport we are involved with and what opportunities it throws up, we are truly blessed. Rather more modestly for myself, I returned from skiing in France and immediately booked a weeks flying in Algo in a months time to try and get some hours built up in the air pre season. Four men of a certain age, all a bit rusty from not flying enough over the past couple of years. Sounds very familiar in our sport!

Fly safe everyone, see you on a hill in the near future hopefully. We are only 6 weeks from the equinox!

sections.title: Safety - Three strikes
sections.content: Safety Officer Rob Urselmann reports

subsections.title: Are holes lining up ?
subsections.content:
Have you ever launched, only to realise some strap wasn’t done up, you forgot your helmet, or your speedbar wasn’t connected? Ever gone flying after a bad night’s sleep, after a long flight and seriously jetlagged, or with a bad cold? Ever got really cold, or really hot, whilst flying to the point it’s hard to be sharp?  Are conditions particularly spicy?

I had all these things happen to me, and they are a signal that I’m likely not 100% on the ball or at the edge of my skills: I was absent minded, slow brained or hypo/hyperthermic, or any of many other reasons why we might not be on top of our game. For those familiar with the Swiss cheese model of accident causation, this means that the holes in the cheese are lining up, making an accident more likely.

In an attempt to have a simple method, and manage my own (over-)enthusiasm, I have been operating my own Three Strikes rule for a few years.

subsections.title: Three strikes = out
subsections.content:
• One of above: I take note and pay attention.
  • Two happen: I stop, have a break and take a real good look at myself. I might decide things are too ‘wobbly’ and it’s not a good day to fly after all.
  • Three things: I take that as a red light and time to call it quits (either abort launch or look for a landing spot).

Clearly, it doesn’t protect one from all incidents, but hopefully it might give you a framework to have a serious look when things aren’t going optimal. I have certainly caught myself a few times and realised it was not a good day for flying (if i’m lucky I caught that whilst still at home!) or that it was time to land.

subsections.title: The other side of an accident:
subsections.content: If you’re going overseas for your winter flying, please read the small print on your travel insurance: many do NOT cover PG anymore, others do NOT cover search&rescue (chopper) and/or repatriation. Even IF your medical treatment is covered, these other costs are £10k at the low end and can top £100k.

subsections.title: Reserve Repack
subsections.content:
I’m curious as to why there was such low uptake for the club reserve repack, despite substantial sponsorship by the club. £25 to really get to grips with what you might rely your life on seems peanuts to me.

I will be running a survey in the coming weeks and it would be appreciated if you took a few seconds to tick your box.

sections.title: Sites Tour - 21 Feb 26
sections.content:
Martin Baxter reports

I’m offering to organise a tour of local sites around Hawes, mainly for newbies but also for pilots new to the area.  We’ll cover basic site guide information including where to park, take-off, landing, routes in between, hazards and top tips.  I’m deliberately organising it at a time of year when we’re unlikely to get distracted by some actual flying.  The date is fixed so that you can plan ahead.

Timings as follows in case you want to join/leave at any point:

1030 - Meet at Dales Countryside Museum car park in Hawes

1120 - Tailbridge

1205 - Stags Fell

1315 - Semer Water

1430 - Wether Fell

1530 - Dodd Fell

1700 - Sunset/debrief/depart

Meeting point at each site is the car park in the Sites Guide.  Dress for cold and wet, although there will be more driving than walking (minimal).  Flask, butties; and beer tokens if you're that way inclined.

If you’re interested then I’ll add you to the event WhatsApp group that we’ll use to co-ordinate things.

 o75six8 57four64o

sections.title: Club Night - Thursday 5th February
sections.content:
Mike B reports

We will be welcoming British Paragliding Champion Richard Butterworth to our next club night to hear all about his comp season of 2025 and the highs and lows of flying the PWC China and British Championships Macedonia!

Remember the earlier start of 7:30pm with finish no later than 9pm and a beer break somewhere in between! This worked really well for everyone in January so we will continue with this format. You can also take food into the function room. Drinks from 7pm in the bar area or function room.

sections.title: Tales from India
sections.content:
John Edmonds reports

I’ve done a couple of trips and our editor in chief, my son, Joseph, has been poking me in the ribs to write something down but you know what it’s like, always something to do! Well this trip I’m organised, not looking for free time at home just occupying the bits of space here on this trip to Kamshet, India!

India, ah a land of mystique and spices, been on my bucket list for ages and here we are. After research we chose Fly Nirvana and Native Place, It’s a package, room, board and internet. We are using their transport and I am getting the benefit of their guidance. They run a successful training school here too, Fly Nirvana, there was a piece on them in Cross Country and that helped  us choose our destination.

So first, India and my first impression, busy, noisy, hazy, full on. We landed at Mumbai and a lift had been organised, straight into the traffic and what a shock. The only thing which has to pass a test is the horn! I’m sure they all understand the need for it, the tooting didn’t seem to make progress any faster, just noisier.

The traffic thinned as we left Mumbai and its conurbation then increased again as we approached Kamshet town, people everywhere, scooters, bikes, lorries, dogs, I’m pleased I wasn’t driving. Native Place is a 20 minute rattle down the road and is quite an oasis. Astrid and Sanjay have been curating this area for 25 years, Astrid planting trees and shrubs while Sanjay engineered a complex building and ran the paragliding training.

John and Sanjay enjoying Chai and Amazing Views from the rooftop terrace.

The building is on land which slopes down to a lake so on several levels with atria and roof terraces, I’m impressed. The garden planting has parts which seem quite wild with cropped beds here and there in between.

Joseph is quite fond of Indian cuisine and is not disappointed here with fresh herbs from the garden, that’s all I say. I’m loving the chai and we have no signs of the dreaded Dheli thingy!

We’re here for a while so there was no need to rush to get things done so after a day acclimatising I joined a group of students on their training hill to polish my ground handling, a real weak point for me. It was busy on this small site with 15 students all racing to get their top to bottoms so Joseph took me to one side where there was space, the down side was that the hard ground was rutted and sloped considerably so soon a pull up had me backing down the hill and falling over, not a good start. I don't want to dwell on this…. I followed the students with a nice fly to the bottom where I found a flatter space to continue my ground handling practice. The weather moves fast here as the temperature races up the thermometer so pretty soon there were thermals pulling the wind and me in different directions, all good practice I told myself! The session which left base at 6am wrapped up by 12 with the students returning to Native Place

I chose to dive up to another site, Tower Hill with Joseph without my glider. He had buddied up with Sanjay’s son Sunith, India’s champion pilot, but such an unassuming young man. Sunith flies D’s and CCC and knows the area here well. He and Joseph took off and there were soon radio reports of booming thermals out front. At this site there is airspace and a restriction to 1500m, pushed to 1700m by some. Joseph ‘complained’ that it was hard to get out of the 6up! He pulled away and flew the 10or so km back to base, landing to be greeted by a security guard to escort him off the property.

Sunith, Joseph and Ajay on Tower take off

My next foray was to take my glider up to the Tower TO, the area there is broad and flat, again to get to grips with this bag of washing on the ground. There was modest success and with the instructors around I was able to take of and fly around in the easy lift for 20 minutes then complete my first top landing. I added my flight deck and flew around for a further 72minutes, all good and smiles landing in the bottom field.

Onto the next day to a site called Shella taking the westerly. A ricketty drive to the parking then a hike along the front then up to an unusual TO about ⅓ up the slope. Here I contributed to the local economy paying a fit young lad to carry my glider. Joseph and I left 2 boys with our gliders, they said ‘go on’, which we did wondering if there was a good market for 2nd hand gliders, ‘we’ll catch you up’ and they did! After taking off it was quickly turn to make the most of the ridge lift then work up and start to use the ample thermals. Atop this ridge are a dozen or so wind turbines but safely set back, you couldn’t miss them so no excuses. I was able to 360 to a good 200m above the tops but stayed well out in front. Joseph zoomed off again and made it to Native Place again, no reports of upset locals this time!

Steve, Ajay, Joseph and John enjoying a Dosa at the Rangolo restaurant - the home base for getting rides up to take off

I’m still not happy with my control on the ground and Joseph confirms this telling me I’m crap at it so another day to the training hill where I achieved a pull up, turn and controlled walk/trot for 20m with the glider where it should be, and…and I got it back down where I wanted it!. I will try to add pictures to make all the schools in the UK sob, there were 50+ students and instructors at the training hill, it was a Sunday, a day off work and they were making the most of it. Back to my story…..Flushed with my success I went to the Tower TO to join Joseph who I knew had gone there to fly and got a ‘taxi’ ride up. These guys with 4 wheel drives just go for it, a horrible drive up in truth, bounced from pillar to post, £6 for the whole vehicle or a 2 hour hike, er, no contest!

I was rigging on top and Joseph must have seen me so came in to land and help, I hope you all have sons like mine. I really just wanted to fly for a bit and one of the instructors from Fly Nirvana was around so he helped me off.The wind was off to the right so I turned right and kept in that direction but for too long, flew into sink and had to head for the landing field. Too far for me to glide in the sinking air I bombed. Now…. this is fun, the day before when Joseph’s landing was near Native Place a young lad on a motor bike offered him a lift and this was accepted because it was a walk, hot and sweaty. Today Joseph had taken off after me, suffered the same sink except he landed at the right place and waiting there was this young lad, with bike, so Joseph dispatched him to collect me and ferry me to a waiting car, how's that for jammy?

Next day….need a rest….Joseph has gone to fly.

Rest day over and feeling fighting fit again. A relaxing morning then after lunch a 20 minute drive to Shellar again. The young boys are there eager to do the hard work so with my poles in hand I step off to the take off with the boy somewhere. The one who got Joseph’s glider draws the short straw, it’s bigger and heavier but they readily accept the challenge with a smile knowing there’s rupees for them at the end of the flying, you pay when you’ve finished and back at your transport. These boys work hard and there is no reason to try to cheat them of their hard earned money.

The small take off was busy with several tandems giving rides. While waiting the ample lift was shown when one had to make 5 or 6 passes and still needed ground staff to get down safely.

My turn and I’m away, a good take off then the radio bleeps, “your right brake is wrapped round the riser”…how, despite my careful checks can this happen? A tip given later is before take off lift the brake high, until the riser is moving and there should be a clear triangle, arm, brake line and riser, I’ll be polishing that check! Anyway after that wobbly start I had a good 90+ minutes exploring the ridge and lift, some gentle, some a little more interesting. After about an hour I thought I would practice a landing approach, out into the flats then back to the ridge. Each track had me losing a bit then going back up. So for the next 20 minutes I experimented with slow lazy turns, speed bar, figure of 8’s still the same or higher. When I finally set up my approach I went out and gently squeezed back to the ridge and could set up a landing approach. The wind was quite light but still directional and easy to see from the other gliders landing, de rigging and even ground handling. I’d taken a couple of wraps on the brakes, another tip given to me this trip, arms up and a gradual bleed off then right down, arms up, stop, turn and brake, glider neatly on the ground. Now I know this is all bread and butter to you guys but to a novice it is a revelation.

There was a party from Derbyshire we met on the hill and later that evening some came over to chat with Sanjay and Astrid. Me and Joseph went up to say hello to the guests, Judy Leden and Chris Dawes. Judy recognised me, we trained together in the late 70's on hangliders in Wales, we had a laugh reminiscing.

John and Judy on Tower take off

We met the Derbyshire pilots on the Tower take off the next day with Judy keen to offer me encouragement and tips, gratefully accepted and a couple of elongated TTB flights. Joseph joined us after a good flight when the lift eluded him.

 

Sunith showed his skill or luck this day, a 50m save over the landing and he was away and after exploring the sky flew back to Native Place….that's what happens when you polish your flying at every opportunity.

A cautionary tale, I am adding to this journal from a hospital room in Pune. Joseph took off well from Tower but suffered a fall from 4-5m onto the sloping and stoney ground and hurt his back. The pilots around helped stop him sliding further down and got the wing detached. The jungle drums were beating and after 30-40 minutes there were helpers with a back board. We got him from his harness onto the board and moved to safety. A 100+ kilo pilot and board needs a lot of lifters, I counted 12 at one point. The twisty undulating 800m path to the parked vehicles took 20 odd minutes with stops for a rest and the lifters to change sides.

Joseph was in pain but there was help to hand. At Fly Nirvana there had been a group,15, navy men training. To look after them a first aider, none flying, had been allocated and he was able to administer some morphine once Joseph was safely on the back board.

I'm going to end now, still in hospital, Joseph pinned and plated in 4 vertebrae, not sure how the story will end. We have to stay extra days to lower the risk of DVT on the flight home, not quite sure where.

Joseph even though he is reluctant to publish his own work may have to finish this story in next month's thrilling installment!

Two thumbs up, helped by a good dose of morphine
